label: Transient gap-junction blockade makes G. dorotocephala regenerate other species' head shapes
claim: In decapitated Girardia dorotocephala fragments, a transient perturbation of cell-to-cell physiological connectivity with the gap junction blocker octanol can lead to regenerated heads whose shapes stochastically match those of other planarian species (Schmidtea mediterranea, Dugesia japonica, Polycelis felina).
quote: after decapitation in G. dorotocephala, a transient perturbation of physiological connectivity among cells (using the gap junction blocker octanol) can result in regenerated heads with quite different shapes, stochastically matching other known species of planaria (S. mediterranea, D. japonica, and P. felina)
scope: Regenerating pre-tail fragments of genetically wild-type Girardia dorotocephala treated with octanol (123 µM, 3 days)
measurable_quantities: head shape class of regenerates
fraction of regenerates per head-shape class
octanol dose and exposure duration
candidate_data: New planarian regeneration experiments with gap junction blockers and head-shape imaging; planarian resources such as PlanMine for cross-species comparison.

label: Hexanol, which does not block gap junctions, does not alter head shape
claim: In G. dorotocephala, the same 3-day exposure to hexanol, a closely related alcohol that does not efficiently block gap junction channels, does not produce altered head morphologies, consistent with the head-shape change depending on octanol's gap-junction-blocking activity rather than a generalized effect of long-chain alcohols.
quote: The same 3-day treatment with the closely related alcohol, hexanol (6-OH), which does not efficiently block gap junction channels, and subsequent regeneration in water for 7 days, did not produce altered morphologies, consistent with the importance of the GJ-blocking activity of octanol, and not some other generalized effect of long-chain alcohols.
scope: Regenerating G. dorotocephala fragments treated with hexanol versus octanol
measurable_quantities: incidence of altered head morphologies after hexanol versus octanol exposure
gap junction coupling under each alcohol
candidate_data: New planarian regeneration experiments comparing alcohols, ideally with dye-coupling assays of gap junction function.

label: Octanol-induced head shapes are morphometrically closer to the species they resemble
claim: By geometric morphometrics (Procrustes distances), the octanol-induced head shapes of G. dorotocephala regenerates are closer to the wild-type head shapes of the species they resemble than to the wild-type G. dorotocephala head shape.
quote: Comparisons of the Procrustes distances between shape groups (Figure 2A, Table 1) showed that the experimentally derived morphologies were closer in shape to the wild-type morphologies they resembled than the wild-type Girardia dorotocephala head morphology.
scope: Landmark-based head shapes of octanol-treated G. dorotocephala regenerates and wild-type G. dorotocephala, D. japonica, S. mediterranea and P. felina
measurable_quantities: Procrustes distances between head-shape groups
canonical variate scores
centroid size
candidate_data: Head images of wild-type planarian species from museum or lab collections and new images of treated regenerates, analysed with standard geometric morphometrics.

label: Induced head-shape outcomes are stochastic and their frequencies track evolutionary distance
claim: Under identical octanol treatment, G. dorotocephala regenerates take one of several discrete head shapes, and the frequencies of the shapes are unequal and correlate roughly with the evolutionary distance (from rRNA phylogeny) between G. dorotocephala and the species each shape resembles, with shapes of closer relatives (S. mediterranea, D. japonica) more frequent than that of the more distant P. felina.
quote: We conclude that not only are phenotypic outcomes from physiological network perturbation stochastic (as the same treatment leads to one of several discrete shapes among individuals), but the frequencies are not equal and correlate roughly with evolutionary distance between the worm species these heads resemble.
scope: Octanol-treated G. dorotocephala regenerates; four planarian species placed on an rRNA-based tree
measurable_quantities: frequency of each pseudo-species head shape
phylogenetic distance between planarian species
candidate_data: Planarian rRNA and transcriptome sequences in GenBank and PlanMine for phylogenetic distances, plus new counts of induced head-shape frequencies.

label: Gap-junction-perturbed worms also acquire the brain shape of the species they resemble
claim: G. dorotocephala regenerates whose heads resemble another species after octanol treatment also have brain morphologies (length/width ratio, by anti-synapsin staining) resembling the brains of wild-type worms of that species.
quote: Strikingly, we found that pseudo worms possessed brain morphologies that look like the brain morphologies of wild-type worms whose head shapes they resembled (Figure 4D–F) (ANOVA, p < 0.001).
scope: Octanol-treated G. dorotocephala regenerates compared with wild-type G. dorotocephala, D. japonica and S. mediterranea
measurable_quantities: brain length/width ratio
head shape class
candidate_data: Planarian nervous-system immunostaining images (e.g., in the Cell Image Library or new experiments) across species and after treatment.

label: Perturbed worms adopt the anterior stem-cell distribution of the species they resemble
claim: In octanol-treated G. dorotocephala regenerates, the transformation toward another species' head shape extends to the species-characteristic distribution of neoblasts (mitotic stem cells) in the anterior body, and the authors conclude that the patterning processes disrupted by gap junction perturbation also organize the distribution of mitotically active cells.
quote: We conclude that the transformation of G. dorotocephala worms to resemble other species also extends to the species-specific, characteristic internal distribution of their stem cells, and that the patterning processes that are disrupted after GJC perturbation are also responsible for organizing the distribution of mitotically active cells.
scope: Phospho-histone H3-positive neoblasts in the anterior sixth of octanol-treated G. dorotocephala and wild-type G. dorotocephala, D. japonica and S. mediterranea
measurable_quantities: number of H3P-positive cells in the anterior sixth of the body
head shape class
candidate_data: Planarian neoblast single-cell and marker data in PlanMine and the Gene Expression Omnibus, plus new H3P staining across species and treatments.

label: Octanol-treated worms show more isopotential regions, which return to normal by 30 days
claim: Ten days after transient octanol exposure, regenerated G. dorotocephala show more distinct isopotential (membrane-voltage) regions by DiBAC dye imaging than controls, and the number of isopotential regions returns to the wild-type level after 30 days of morphological remodeling.
quote: We detected an increased number of isopotential regions in the pseudo worms compared to the states of control worms; interestingly, the numbers of isopotential regions return to those of a wild-type state after 30 days of morphological remodeling (Figure 6I).
scope: Whole-body DiBAC4(3) voltage-dye images of octanol-treated and control G. dorotocephala at 10 and 30 days
measurable_quantities: number of distinct isopotential regions per worm
relative membrane potential (DiBAC fluorescence)
days after treatment
candidate_data: New voltage-dye imaging of planarians; no public planarian bioelectric imaging dataset is known.

label: Brief gap-junction blockade persistently alters bioelectric network state after drug washout
claim: In G. dorotocephala, the long-lasting alteration of bioelectric patterning after brief octanol exposure is not caused by residual octanol (which leaves tissues within 24 h) but is initiated by octanol's disruption of gap junction communication, which alters bioelectric network topology and results in a persistent perturbation of bioelectric state.
quote: Although these long-lasting alterations in bioelectrical patterning are not directly caused by octanol remaining within the body of the worm (since 8-OH is known to depart planarian tissues within 24 h [20]), they are initiated by the octanol-mediated disruption of GJC, which alters bioelectric network topology, and results in persistent perturbation of bioelectric state.
scope: G. dorotocephala somatic tissues after transient octanol exposure
measurable_quantities: tissue octanol concentration over time
gap junction coupling (dye transfer) over time
isopotential region count
candidate_data: New GC-MS washout measurements combined with time-course dye-coupling and voltage imaging in planarians.

label: Partial, variable gap-junction blockade is consistent with stochastic head-shape outcomes
claim: The variability and overall magnitude of the bioelectric effect imply that octanol only partially shuts down gap junction communication in each G. dorotocephala (affecting some percentage of gap junctions per animal), which the authors consider consistent with the stochasticity of the head-shape phenotype.
quote: The variability and overall magnitude of the effect imply that the result of 8-OH exposure is only partially effective in shutting down GJC (affecting some percentage of GJs in any animal); this is consistent with the stochasticity of the morphological phenotype (Figure 3).
scope: Octanol-treated G. dorotocephala
measurable_quantities: fraction of gap junctions blocked per animal
inter-animal variability of coupling
head-shape outcome per animal
candidate_data: New per-animal coupling measurements paired with head-shape scoring; none known publicly.

label: Induced head shapes remodel back toward G. dorotocephala after regeneration ends
claim: The other-species head shapes induced in G. dorotocephala by octanol are not permanent: between days 10 and 30, after regeneration is complete and without further injury, the heads are remodeled to more closely resemble wild-type G. dorotocephala.
quote: We found that the induced morphologies were remodeled, long after regenerative processes had ended, to produce morphologies that bore closer resemblance to wild-type G. dorotocephala.
scope: Octanol-induced pseudo-species G. dorotocephala photographed daily from day 10 to day 30
measurable_quantities: head shape over time after regeneration
time to return to wild-type shape
candidate_data: New time-lapse imaging of treated planarians with morphometric scoring.

label: Head remodeling follows a path through shape space from S. mediterranea-like to D. japonica-like to normal
claim: In canonical variate shape space, the D. japonica head morphology lies between those of G. dorotocephala and S. mediterranea, and octanol-induced S. mediterranea-like G. dorotocephala heads remodel by moving from S. mediterranea-like to D. japonica-like to G. dorotocephala morphology.
quote: DJ morphology lies between GD and SM morphologies in this space, and we observe remodeling that moves from SM morphology to DJ morphology to GD morphology.
scope: Remodeling octanol-treated G. dorotocephala regenerates, days 10–30
measurable_quantities: canonical variate scores of head shape over time
candidate_data: New longitudinal morphometric data of remodeling planarians alongside wild-type species head images.

label: Planarian morphology behaves as a homeostatic parameter maintained toward a target shape
claim: In planarians, morphology appears to be a homeostatic parameter that is repeatedly assessed and adjusted to maintain a 'target' morphology: after an incorrect head shape is produced during regeneration, the mismatch with the target triggers remodeling (between days 10 and 17 in octanol-treated G. dorotocephala), even after large-scale reorganization has ended.
quote: Morphology appears to be a homeostatic parameter, one that is consistently assessed and adjusted in order to maintain some “target” morphology.
scope: Regenerating and remodeling planarians (G. dorotocephala)
measurable_quantities: onset time of remodeling
deviation of head shape from species-typical shape over time
candidate_data: Time-course planarian imaging and morphometrics; none known publicly.

label: Coherent discrete head shapes show the octanol effect is instructive rather than toxic
claim: The octanol-induced head-shape change in G. dorotocephala is instructive rather than a toxic or housekeeping defect, because it yields one of several coherent, ecologically valid morphologies rather than regeneration failure or disorganized growth, with no intermediate morphologies observed.
quote: The head morphology alteration effect was instructive, and not merely one of toxicity or a house-keeping defect, because the outcome was not merely disruption of regenerative ability or a generalized mis-patterning (e.g., tumor or other disorganized growth), but rather resulted in one of several coherent (and ecologically-valid) morphologies.
scope: Octanol-treated G. dorotocephala regenerates
measurable_quantities: fraction of regenerates with coherent species-like shapes versus intermediate or disorganized shapes
candidate_data: New morphometric data on treated regenerates testing for intermediate shapes.

label: Bioelectric networks are a physiological input deriving distinct morphologies from one genome
claim: Physiological bioelectric networks are a previously unrecognized input by which distinct morphologies, including those of other species, can be derived from the same genome, as shown by gap-junction perturbation in G. dorotocephala.
quote: Here, we identify a novel physiological input into the process by which distinct morphologies can be derived from the same genome: physiological bioelectric networks.
scope: Planarian head regeneration (G. dorotocephala), proposed as a general input to morphogenesis
measurable_quantities: morphological outcome under bioelectric perturbation in isogenic animals
genomic sequence identity between treated and control animals
candidate_data: Planarian genome and transcriptome resources (PlanMine, SmedGD) to confirm genetic identity, combined with new bioelectric perturbation experiments.

label: Agent-based model with migrating and signaling cells reproduces the observed planarian head shapes
claim: In an agent-based model of planarian head regeneration in which static somatic cells emit a chemical signal and migratory cells (neoblasts or their progeny) are repelled by it, deactivating different subsets of signaling cells (representing octanol gap-junction blockade) reproduces the four observed head shapes, so a small set of gap-junction-regulated cell behaviors such as migration and cell-cell signaling can quantitatively explain the observed morphologies.
quote: We conclude that a small set of cell-level behaviors, such as migration and cell-cell signaling that are known to be regulated by GJC and thus are perturbed by octanol exposure [35,39,49,98,101,102], can quantitatively explain the morphologies we observed in planaria.
scope: The authors' two-cell-type agent-based model of the planarian head with an elastic boundary
measurable_quantities: simulated head length and width intervals (L1, L2)
measured head dimensions of real worms
candidate_data: The paper's model description in its supplementary material; new morphometric data from planarians for comparison.

label: Instructive gap-junction-dependent signals pass from somatic tissue to neoblasts during regeneration
claim: The authors propose that significant instructive, gap-junction-dependent signaling passes from planarian somatic tissues to neoblasts or their progeny to guide new tissue generation and shaping during regeneration.
quote: In this model, we propose that significant instructive (GJ-dependent) signaling occurs from the somatic tissues to the neoblasts or their progeny, to guide the new tissue generation and shaping during regeneration.
scope: Regenerating planarian heads
measurable_quantities: innexin expression in somatic cells versus neoblasts
neoblast migration paths after cell-type-specific gap junction knockdown
candidate_data: Planarian single-cell atlases in PlanMine and the Gene Expression Omnibus for innexin expression by cell type; new cell-type-specific RNAi experiments.

label: Planarian head shapes may be attractors of a gap-junction-coupled bioelectric network
claim: The authors hypothesize that distinct planarian head shapes may be attractors in the state space of the bioelectric network formed by body cells coupled by gap junctions, that these attractors correspond to regions of morphospace in the evolutionary sense, and that octanol knocks the network's stochastic dynamics into one of several nearby attractors normally belonging to other flatworm species.
quote: We hypothesize that distinct shape outcomes may be attractors in a state space describing distinct modes of the bioelectric network of planarian body cells connected by gap junctions (electrical synapses); in essence, these attractors correspond to regions of a morphospace as classically understood by evolutionary theory [151].
scope: Planarian body-wide bioelectric networks (G. dorotocephala and related species)
measurable_quantities: multistability of simulated or measured bioelectric network states
mapping of network states to head shapes
candidate_data: None known; would require new bioelectric network models and cell-resolution voltage time series.

label: Regeneration as descent to a low free-energy attractor, with induced shapes as local minima
claim: On the authors' proposed view, discrete planarian head patterns are the lowest free-energy outcomes of bioelectric network dynamics; amputation raises free energy and regeneration is a return to a low-energy attractor, octanol shifts the system to another attractor, and the induced other-species shapes are only local minima since worms return to the global minimum of G. dorotocephala morphology after about 3–4 weeks.
quote: On this view (Figure 9), the discrete head patterns are outcomes of bioelectric network dynamics with the lowest free-energy; cutting the network raises the free energy by deviating the system from its optimal morphology (damage), and initiates the regenerative process—a journey back down to a low-energy attractor.
scope: Planarian regeneration conceived as dynamics of a bioelectric network
candidate_data: None known.

label: Somatic cells can be modeled as a slow neural-like network obeying brain-like dynamics
claim: The authors propose conceptualizing the link between gap junctional connectivity among planarian cells and discrete regenerative outcomes by viewing the cells as a neural-like network that processes developmental information more slowly but obeys the same statistical dynamics as the brain.
quote: Thus, we propose that one way to conceptualize the linkage between bioelectrical connectivity among worm cells (GJC) and discrete global behavioral outcomes achieved by regeneration is to view the worms’ cells as a neural-like network, processing developmental information more slowly but obeying the same statistical dynamics rules as are known to occur in the brain (Figure 9A).
scope: Planarian somatic cell networks during regeneration
candidate_data: None known.

label: Head shape may be encoded in time-dependent rather than steady voltage patterns
claim: Because single-image voltage distributions showed no simple correspondence with the head shapes of octanol-treated G. dorotocephala, the authors consider it most likely that shape outcomes are encoded in time-dependent bioelectric activity rather than in steady voltage distributions, as in information encoding in the central nervous system.
quote: The most likely explanation however is that shape outcomes may not be encoded via steady (single-image) distributions but in time-dependent activity, as occurs during information encoding in the central nervous system.
scope: Planarian bioelectric patterns and head-shape outcomes
measurable_quantities: time series of membrane voltage across planarian tissue
head shape outcome
candidate_data: New voltage-imaging movies of regenerating planarians; none known publicly.

label: Evolutionary distance among planarians may reflect ease of shifting a shared patterning network
claim: The authors suggest that a core network of gene-regulatory elements and gap-junction-mediated signals may be shared among many planarians, with species differences tweaking its dynamics, so that evolutionary distance between planarian species may reflect how easily this network can be shifted into its different outcome states, as during gap junction inhibition.
quote: The evolutionary distance among the planarian types may thus be expected to reflect the ease of shifting this network into its different potential outcome states (as occurs during GJC inhibition).
scope: Planarian species (Girardia, Dugesia, Schmidtea, Polycelis/Phagocata)
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic distance between species
frequency with which perturbation of one species yields another's morphology
candidate_data: Planarian phylogenies from GenBank sequences and PlanMine transcriptomes, combined with new perturbation experiments across several species.

label: Embryonic nicotine exposure causes major brain malformations in Xenopus
claim: Exposing Xenopus laevis embryos to nicotine (0.1 mg/mL, stages 10–35) causes major brain morphology defects (absent nostrils, forebrain or midbrain, misformed hindbrain) in about 55% of tadpoles at stage 45, compared with about 6% of controls.
quote: Nicotine exposure caused a significantly high incidence of major brain morphology defects (~55%) in comparison to controls (~6%).
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos exposed to 0.1 mg/mL nicotine from stage 10 to 35, scored at stage 45
measurable_quantities: incidence of brain morphology defects
nicotine concentration and exposure window
candidate_data: Xenbase phenotype and anatomy resources plus new Xenopus teratogen exposure experiments.

label: BETSE model: leak and Kir channels produce a hyperpolarized neural tube prepattern
claim: In a BETSE bioelectric model of the stage 15 Xenopus neurula, regional differences in K+ and Cl− leak permeability open Kir channels in the neural tube, producing a Vmem of about −50 mV there while the neural folds and ectoderm stay near −5 mV, matching observed embryonic Vmem patterns.
quote: This results in open Kir channels in the hyperpolarized neural tube region leading to a Vmem pattern of approximately −50 mV in the neural tube region, while the lateral neural folds and ectoderm remain at ~−5 mV (Fig. 3a, e).
scope: BETSE model of an anterior view of the stage 15 Xenopus neurula surface in 0.1× MMR
measurable_quantities: resting membrane potential of neural tube cells
resting membrane potential of neural fold and ectoderm cells
candidate_data: Xenopus electrophysiology recordings and voltage-dye imaging; Xenbase expression data for Kir and leak channel genes.

label: Nicotine depolarizes the neural plate prepattern by about 15 mV, as the model predicted
claim: In stage 15 Xenopus embryos, nicotine treatment significantly reduces the endogenous neural hyperpolarization signal (a depolarization of about 15 mV, measured by calibrated voltage-dye imaging), matching the BETSE model's prediction in direction and magnitude.
quote: Nicotine-treated embryos showed significant reduction in endogenous neural Vmem signal (depolarization by ~15 mV) in comparison to controls (Figs. 4a, b, e, f, and Supplementary Figure 1). This observation matches the BETSE model predictions of nicotine effect on Vmem both in direction (depolarization) and magnitude (~15 mV).
scope: Neural plate and flanking ectoderm of stage 15 Xenopus laevis embryos exposed to nicotine
measurable_quantities: neural plate Vmem (CC2-DMPE:DiBAC4(3) ratio calibrated by whole-cell recordings)
Vmem difference between neural plate and ectoderm
candidate_data: New Xenopus voltage-dye imaging and intracellular recordings under nicotine.

label: Nicotine causes brain defects by disrupting the endogenous bioelectric prepattern
claim: The authors' BETSE model explains nicotine-induced brain defects in Xenopus as resulting from nicotine's disruption of the endogenous bioelectric prepattern (neural tube hyperpolarization) required for brain development.
quote: Our model explains why nicotine induces brain defects: it correctly predicts the disruptive effects of this teratogen on the endogenous bioelectric prepattern required for brain development.
scope: Xenopus laevis neurula and brain development under nicotine exposure
measurable_quantities: neural tube Vmem
incidence of brain defects
correlation between Vmem disruption and defects in individual embryos
candidate_data: New paired voltage imaging and brain-morphology scoring in Xenopus; Xenbase for channel and receptor expression.

label: Normal brain patterning requires the differential Vmem between neural tube and lateral tissue
claim: In Xenopus brain development, it is the spatial contrast of Vmem that matters: depolarizing the neural tube region or hyperpolarizing the lateral regions both cause brain defects, because the precise differential bioelectric state induces the balance of proliferation, apoptosis and gene expression needed to build a normal brain.
quote: The spatial patterning is crucial, as both depolarization of the middle region, or hyperpolarization of the lateral regions, both cause brain defects—it is the precise differential bioelectric state that induces the required balance of proliferation, apoptosis, and gene expression to build a normal brain28,48.
scope: Neural tube and surrounding ectoderm of Xenopus neurula-stage embryos
measurable_quantities: Vmem of neural tube and lateral regions
proliferation and apoptosis rates
brain-patterning gene expression
brain defect incidence
candidate_data: Xenbase gene expression data and new region-specific Vmem manipulation experiments in Xenopus.

label: BETSE model predicts HCN2 maintains the neural tube Vmem pattern despite nicotine
claim: The BETSE model predicts that uniformly expressed HCN2 channels, which open at hyperpolarized Vmem and so amplify small Vmem gradients, open preferentially in the Xenopus neural tube and maintain its hyperpolarized Vmem pattern even in nicotine-exposed model embryos.
quote: Importantly, our model predicts that HCN2 expression leads to maintenance of neural tube Vmem pattern even in nicotine-exposed model embryos, similar to the action of IT (Fig. 3c vs. d, e, f).
scope: BETSE model of the Xenopus neurula with HCN2 channels (mouse kinetics, Na+:K+ permeability ratio 0.2) and nicotine
measurable_quantities: simulated neural tube Vmem with and without HCN2 and nicotine
simulated lateral-region Vmem
candidate_data: BETSE simulation software (open source) to rerun the model; new Xenopus voltage measurements.
